title: Vertical: Production Single-Family (302 Units)
summary: 302 houses is not 302 construction projects — it's a manufacturing problem. This module covers the Bahamian concrete house sequence, even-flow production scheduling, the island's finite trade labor pool, and the materials discipline that island logistics forces on you.

sections.heading: The Bahamian house, step by step
sections.body: Reinforced concrete/CMU dominates. Per unit: layout → footings (shallow, on rock — often minimal excavation, sometimes pinned/doweled to rock; limestone bearing is superb) → slab on grade with plumbing rough-in cast in → block walls with poured reinforced columns and ring beam → roof structure (hurricane-strapped timber or engineered trusses; concrete flat roofs on some typologies) → roof covering (metal standing seam preferred for wind and insurance) → impact-rated or shuttered windows/doors → MEP rough → insulation/furring → interior finishes → exterior render/paint → fixtures → punch → inspections → Occupancy Certificate. Per-house cycle: 60–120 working days.

sections.heading: Production management: the takt
sections.body: Standardize 3–6 floor plans. Release starts at a steady weekly rate matched to your SLOWEST trade's capacity — not to sales enthusiasm. Each sub moves house-to-house on a takt (a block crew lays 400–700 blocks/day and does one house per X days — this rhythm is the core production math). QC by sampling plus hold points: EVERY house gets checked at footing/rebar, ring beam, roof strapping, and MEP rough; finish tolerances get sampled. A superintendent covers 15–30 active units, so at a 60–80 unit peak you run 3–4 supers under you.

sections.heading: Labor: the island has a ceiling
sections.body: New Providence has deep masonry and concrete trades but finite capacity. Running 60+ concurrent homes strains the island's block-laying and finishing pools and pushes wages up — accelerating starts raises unit labor cost AND drops quality scores. Minimum wage is BSD $260/week; skilled trades run far above; NIB employer contributions apply to direct labor; every sub must hold a business licence. The escape valves — work permits for foreign crews — run 4–8+ weeks each and are politically visible.

sections.heading: Materials: buyout, staging, and shrinkage
sections.body: Island logistics demand buyout discipline: bulk-purchase block, cement (duty-free since 2025), rebar, and trusses per phase, ahead of need. Run a fenced, cameraed materials compound with inventory control — theft shrinkage is a real Caribbean line item; budget 1–2%. A common Bahamian model: developer-supplied materials with LABOR-ONLY trade subs — it protects you from sub-side material markup and theft, at the price of running procurement yourself.

quiz.teach: The Bahamian concrete house has a fixed structural logic — each stage bears on the one before.
items: Footings on rock and slab with plumbing rough-in cast in
Block walls with reinforced columns and ring beam
quiz.explanation: Concrete from the ground up, dry-in before interior trades, finishes last, and the OC — the document that lets the buyer close — at the end. Every house in the program walks this same path; production management is keeping 60+ of them walking it in step.

quiz.teach: Even-flow production releases starts at a constant rate. The question is what rate.
quiz.prompt: Sales pace doubles. The sales director wants starts doubled. What sets the actual ceiling on your start rate?

choices.text: Your slowest trade's real capacity — plus super coverage and QC integrity; exceeding it buys wage inflation and quality failures, not faster delivery
choices.why: Correct. Starts released beyond trade capacity just queue up half-built — while pushing island wages up and first-pass inspection rates down.

choices.text: Nothing — sales funds construction, so sales sets pace
choices.why: Sales sets the CEILING of what you should build, not the rate you CAN build. The island's block-laying pool doesn't expand because your sales office had a good quarter.
Financing paces cash, and it matters — but the binding physical constraint on this island is trade labor capacity.
Cement is duty-free and block is made locally; materials scale with purchase orders. Skilled labor doesn't.

quiz.explanation: The correct response to doubled sales is a MEASURED ramp: extend trade partnerships, add a super before adding his units, open the work-permit pipeline as a backup, and raise starts only as verified capacity arrives. Presold backlog is a nice problem; 70 stalled slabs is not.

quiz.teach: Two models for trade contracts: turnkey (sub supplies labor + materials) vs labor-only (you supply materials).
quiz.prompt: Why is developer-supplied-materials / labor-only subcontracting a common Bahamian production model?

choices.text: It strips out sub-side material markup and theft exposure, and puts island procurement (the hard part) under the party with the most leverage — you
choices.why: Correct. At 302 houses your bulk purchasing beats any sub's pricing, and materials in YOUR fenced compound shrink less than materials in twenty pickup trucks.
Quality comes from your hold points and first-pass tracking, not the contract form. The model's win is commercial: markup and shrinkage control.

choices.text: Bahamian law restricts subs from importing materials
choices.why: No such restriction — subs can and do buy materials. It's a choice about margin and control, not compliance.

choices.text: It transfers schedule risk to the developer's suppliers
choices.why: Backwards — it takes procurement risk ONTO you. That's the price you pay for capturing the margin; the administrative load is real.

quiz.explanation: The trade-off is margin control vs administrative load: labor-only means you run buyout, staging, inventory, and the compound. Worth it at production scale IF you build the clerical machine to match — which is exactly the developer skillset this whole program trains.

quiz.teach: Quality on a production program is enforced at hold points — stages where work may not proceed without sign-off.
quiz.prompt: A block sub's ring beams fail inspection twice in a row. Remove them (schedule hit) or supervise-and-remediate (risk)?

choices.text: Escalate structurally: stop their new starts, remediate under direct supervision, and re-qualify them at reduced volume — with removal as the explicit next step
choices.why: Correct. Two consecutive structural failures is a pattern, not an accident. Contain (no new starts), fix (supervised remediation), then either verified recovery or removal.

choices.text: Remove them immediately — structural failures are unforgivable
choices.why: Defensible but expensive on an island with 2–3 subs per trade: instant removal mid-phase can cost more schedule than a controlled probation, and Nassau's market is small enough that scorched earth has a memory.
Remediating while they keep producing at full speed means your supervision chases their output. Containment first — the failing crew doesn't get MORE houses.

choices.text: Waive the inspections — the engineer can recertify later
choices.why: The ring beam is the hurricane structure. Waiving a structural hold point on a wind-zone island is the one option that should genuinely never be on the table.

quiz.explanation: This is why you keep 2–3 competing subs per trade: so no single sub can hold the schedule hostage while you enforce quality. Publish first-pass inspection rates per sub — nothing improves masonry like a league table.

quiz.teach: At production scale, the developer's org chart is mostly systems, not trades.
quiz.prompt: Subcontract or direct-manage each element of the 302-house program:

items.scope: Masonry, roofing, MEP, and finish trades
items.why: Every trade is subcontracted — ideally 2–3 competing subs per trade so no one holds the schedule hostage.

items.scope: The production schedule and weekly start releases
items.why: The takt IS the program. Releasing starts is the developer's throttle on cash, labor, and quality — never delegated.

items.scope: Bulk buyout of block, cement, rebar, trusses
items.why: Island logistics + the labor-only model put procurement on your desk, where the volume leverage lives.
This is the revenue pipeline — OC throughput converts construction into cash, and only the developer feels that urgency.
Run the warranty program with your own coordinator calling back the responsible subs — owners' warranty experience is your reputation in a small market.

quiz.explanation: Trades build houses; the developer builds the machine that builds houses — schedule, procurement, QC, permits, closings, warranty. If you're personally laying out footings, something upstream has failed.

mathProblems.title: One production house, hard cost
mathProblems.context: Production-spec hard cost on New Providence runs $190–280/sf in the current market — meaningfully above South Florida, driven by freight, duty, and logistics.

mathProblems.title: Superintendent headcount
mathProblems.context: A super covers 15–30 active units depending on complexity and travel time. Understaffing shows up in first-pass inspection rates, not in the budget — until rework.

mathProblems.title: Block crew takt
mathProblems.context: Takt math: each crew takes a fixed time per house, crews run in parallel, and the phase duration follows. This is the production mini-game's core arithmetic.

mathProblems.title: Vertical Phase 2 hard cost
mathProblems.context: A phase estimate: houses at $/sf plus the general-conditions burn for the phase duration, then the production-vertical contingency tier (5–8%).

decisionPoints.title: The best block sub wants an advance
decisionPoints.scenario: Your highest-quality block sub — first-pass rate 96%, never missed a takt slot — asks for a $150K materials advance to carry them through a cash crunch caused by another developer paying late. Your options range from a straight advance to letting them stew. Nassau is a small market and this conversation will be remembered.

options.label: Solve their interest, not their position: milestone-based early payments against materials delivered to YOUR compound, plus faster payment terms going forward
options.outcome: They get cash-flow certainty (the real need), you get security (the materials are on your site, in your inventory), and the market hears you stood by a good sub without becoming their bank. The relationship compounds for years.

options.label: Wire the $150K advance against future work
options.outcome: Generous and fast — and unsecured. If their crunch deepens (their other client still isn't paying), your advance is an unsecured loan to an insolvent sub. Kindness without structure is exposure.

options.label: Refuse — their cash flow is their problem
options.outcome: Contractually correct. Three weeks later your best crew is pouring someone else's ring beams while their company restructures, your takt slips program-wide, and the story of how you treat good subs in trouble travels the whole island.

decisionPoints.debrief: Module 13 in action: the position is 'advance me $150K'; the interest is cash-flow certainty. Milestone payments against delivered materials meet the interest with a fraction of the exposure. And the relationship horizon matters — in a small market, being the developer good subs can rely on is a compounding asset.

decisionPoints.title: Model homes: build ahead or build real?
decisionPoints.scenario: Sales needs model homes for the launch. Option A: pull three houses from Phase 1 forward, before roads and permanent power reach them — generator power, temporary access, built out of sequence. Option B: hold the launch until the first street is genuinely finished — roads, lights, landscape, three furnished models on it.

options.label: Hold for one genuinely finished street with models on it
options.outcome: Later launch, vastly stronger product: buyers walk a real street of the real community, not a construction site with three furnished islands. The finished streetscape sells the master plan, and the models were built in sequence at normal cost.

options.label: Build three models out of sequence on generators
options.outcome: The models open months earlier and cost 20–30% more each (temporary power, out-of-sequence trades, damaged access repaved). Buyers tour a construction zone — and the discount their offers imply prices exactly that experience.

options.label: Sell from renders and a sales center only
options.outcome: Cheapest — and at this price point, weakest. Palm Cay's lesson cuts both ways: buyers on this island have been burned by developers selling paper. Physical proof is what converts at premium pricing.

decisionPoints.debrief: Amenities and models sell the units that fund everything — but out-of-sequence construction always carries a premium and a quality tax. The strongest sales tool this market knows is a finished street: it proves the infrastructure, the product, AND the developer, all at once.
